question: What best describes disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: A one-time survey conducted during a major crisis
options.B: A clinical trial testing new hospital equipment
options.C: A research study on the cure for chronic diseases
options.D: An ongoing and systematic collection of health data

explanation: Surveillance requires continuous monitoring and data gathering over time, unlike a single survey or short-term research trial. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h1)

question: Why is disease surveillance often called an early warning system?

options.A: It predicts exact weather conditions for disease outbreaks.
options.B: It helps health workers spot unusual patterns before an epidemic grows.
options.C: It automatically cures patients before they visit the hospital.
options.D: It replaces the need for laboratory testing entirely.

explanation: Spotting rising cases early lets health workers jump in and take action before a tiny bump turns into a full-blown outbreak! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h1)

question: What is the main goal of gathering public health surveillance data?

options.A: To guide health policy and practical actions
options.B: To increase the cost of medical treatments
options.C: To punish clinics that report too many sick patients
options.D: To fill up hospital filing cabinets with paperwork

explanation: We don't collect health data just to sit on shelves! It's meant to be put to work for planning and stopping diseases in our communities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h2)

question: How does surveillance help us check if a vaccination campaign worked?

options.A: By calculating the exact salary of the nurses giving the shots
options.B: By showing whether disease rates drop after the vaccines are given
options.C: By tracking how many nurses attended the training workshop
options.D: By testing the chemical composition of vaccine vials

explanation: By keeping track of sickness rates over time, public health teams can easily tell if giving out those vaccines actually stopped the disease. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h2)

question: What happens in passive surveillance?

options.A: Patients must call a special hotline to report their own illness.
options.B: Health workers actively visit every household in the village.
options.C: Data is only collected during a national census every ten years.
options.D: Clinics send routine reports without being pushed by health officers.

explanation: Think of passive surveillance as your local clinic doing what they normally do—sending in their regular reports as part of daily duty without waiting for someone to chase them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h3)

question: When would the Ministry of Health use syndromic surveillance?

options.A: When they want to check the exact financial budget of a rural hospital
options.B: When they need the absolute fastest warning about a potential outbreak based on symptoms
options.C: When laboratory tests are cheap and results are ready within minutes
options.D: When they need a complete census of all chronic illnesses

explanation: Syndromic surveillance watches out for symptom groups (like sudden fever and rashes) even before lab results come back, giving us a super-fast early alarm! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h3)

question: What is the very first step in the disease surveillance cycle?
explanation: It all starts right at the frontline! Nurses and health workers spot and record cases, kicking off the whole surveillance process. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h4)

question: Why is 'dissemination' an important step in surveillance?

options.A: It stops patients from visiting primary health care clinics.
options.B: It permanently deletes old health records to save computer space.
options.C: It ensures feedback is shared with the workers and leaders who need to take action.
options.D: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies make a profit.

explanation: Dissemination just means sharing the news back. It closes the loop so the people who collected the data and the ones who need to fight the disease are on the same page! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h4)

question: Which of these is a main source of laboratory-based surveillance data?

options.A: Confirmation of specific germs and drug resistance patterns
options.B: Commercial market prices for staple foods
options.C: Records of primary school student attendance
options.D: Daily weather forecasts and rainfall measurements

explanation: The lab tells us the exact culprit making people sick and whether standard drugs can fight it off or if the germ is resistant. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h5)

question: Why are vital statistics like death registries important for health surveillance?

options.A: They measure the trading volume of the local agricultural market.
options.B: They calculate the daily water supply pressure in the city.
options.C: They help track causes of death and overall population health trends.
options.D: They show which political party won the local government election.

explanation: Death registries give us a big-picture view of what is really killing people in our communities, guiding where public health help is needed most. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h5)

question: What event usually triggers an immediate public health outbreak investigation?

options.A: An annual audit of the hospital electricity bill
options.B: The routine retirement of a senior hospital administrator
options.C: The delivery of new office furniture to the clinic
options.D: A sudden jump in disease cases above the normal level

explanation: When we suddenly see way more sick people than we normally expect in an area, that's our cue to investigate right away! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h6)

question: Why should outbreak control measures sometimes start before lab results are fully finalized?

options.A: To avoid paperwork and administrative meetings
options.B: Because laboratory tests are always completely inaccurate
options.C: Because doctors are not allowed to read lab reports
options.D: To prevent further spread and save lives immediately

explanation: Waiting for lab work during a fast-moving crisis can cost lives. Taking action early based on clinical signs is a lifesaver! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h6)

question: What makes primary health care nurses so crucial for disease surveillance?

options.A: They are responsible for funding national health budgets.
options.B: They manufacture all the vaccines used in the country.
options.C: They write the international guidelines for disease control.
options.D: They interact directly with patients daily and spot early signs of disease.

explanation: As frontline nurses, you are the eyes and ears of health surveillance because you see the patients first every single day! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h7)

question: A community health nurse notices three children from the same compound presenting with watery diarrhea and vomiting. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Treat the patients, stabilize them, and report the suspected cholera cases to local authorities
options.B: Close down the entire primary health care clinic until next week
options.C: Tell the parents to stay home and wait to see if the symptoms go away on their own
options.D: Send a formal letter to an international health organization via postal mail

explanation: Great nursing care means treating the patient right in front of you while also sounding the alarm to protect the whole community from a potential outbreak. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h7)

question: Which of these is NOT a common challenge in disease surveillance?

options.A: Fear of social stigma and discrimination in communities
options.B: An overabundance of fully trained staff and limitless financial funding
options.C: Poor infrastructure like unreliable internet and transport
options.D: Underreporting of cases by busy or overworked clinical staff

explanation: If only we had endless money and staff! In reality, health systems always struggle with shortages, not an overabundance of funding. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h8)

question: How does community stigma negatively affect disease surveillance data?

options.A: It speeds up the transmission of weekly health reports to the capital.
options.B: It causes people to hide sick family members and avoid visiting clinics.
options.C: It automatically increases the national budget allocation for health.
options.D: It forces laboratories to buy more expensive testing equipment.

explanation: When people are scared of being judged or isolated, they hide their illnesses at home, leading to missing cases and inaccurate health stats. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T93#GNS214_U1_T93_h8)
